title: Rivers and Lakes
summary: Tunely, a music-streaming app, needs royalty reports and a live trending chart from the same flood of plays. When do you process data in big nightly batches, and when as a never-ending stream?

goals.text: Move analytics off the production database
Explain how a MapReduce-style batch job works
Count a stream with windows and watermarks
Compare the lambda and kappa architectures

steps.title: Ask the production database
body: Tunely streams music. Every play is a row in Postgres — the same database that handles logins and playlists. Artists want to know their play counts, so the analysts run GROUP BY song straight against it.
With two million plays a day the query takes a few seconds, the numbers are live and exact, and nobody notices the extra load. Simple, and fine for now.

steps.title: Reports versus listeners
body: Two years later it's sixty million plays a day. The royalty report now scans billions of rows for forty minutes, evicting the hot data from cache and soaking up disk bandwidth.

Listeners pay for it: pressing play times out because the database is busy answering an analyst. Analytical queries — read everything, aggregate — and transactional queries — touch a few rows, fast — want very different machines.

callout.text: Never let reporting share a database with the user-facing path. Even a replica only moves the problem once scans get big enough.

steps.title: A lake and a nightly job
body: Tunely stops storing plays in Postgres. Each play becomes an event on a log, landed every hour as files in cheap object storage — a data lake that keeps the raw history forever.

Every night a batch job reads all of yesterday's files, computes exact totals per song and artist, and loads them into a warehouse built for big scans. Analysts query the warehouse; production never sees them.
changes: + Play events go to an event log

steps.title: Split, shuffle, sum
body: How do you count 60 million plays quickly? Split the files across many workers. In the map step each worker turns its plays into pairs like (song, 1). The framework then shuffles, sending every pair for the same song to the same reducer.
Each reduce worker sums its songs and writes totals. Add machines and the job gets faster; if one dies, only its slice reruns. Modern engines like Spark refine the idea, but the shape is the same.

steps.title: Trending, as of yesterday
body: Product wants a Trending now chart. A song goes viral at lunchtime — and the chart, fed by last night's job, won't show it until tomorrow morning.
Running the batch every hour helps a little but rescans hours of data each time, and the chart is still up to an hour behind. Batch is great at complete and exact; it's bad at now.
changes: ~ Chart is up to a day old

steps.title: Process events as they flow
body: A stream processor reads the same event log continuously. It keeps a small running count per song in memory and, every minute, writes the latest numbers to a fast Trending store.

Instead of re-reading the past, it updates state one event at a time, so the chart is seconds old. The processor checkpoints its state and log position, so after a crash it resumes without double-counting.
changes: + Stream processor reads the event log
~ Trending chart reads the stream's output

steps.title: A stream never ends — so cut it
body: You can't ask "how many plays in total?" of an endless stream. Instead you count inside windows: slices of time that open, collect events and close with a result.
Pick the shape to fit the question: tumbling windows for per-minute charts, sliding windows for "last ten minutes", session windows for a listener's continuous listening.

card.title: Three kinds of window
lines: # plays per song, grouped by time

bars.label: Session
bars.note: until a listener goes quiet for 30 min

steps.title: Plays from the past
body: A listener on a plane plays ten songs offline at 14:05; the phone uploads them at 16:40. Which window do they count in? By event time they belong to 14:05 — a window that closed long ago.

A watermark is the processor's guess that "everything before 16:39 has probably arrived". Windows wait a grace period past it, then close. Later stragglers are dropped or sent as corrections — fast results are slightly inexact.
changes: + Offline phone uploads plays 2½ hours late
~ Very late plays miss their window

steps.title: Both rivers: lambda
body: The lambda architecture runs both: a stream for fast, approximate numbers, and the nightly batch that recomputes exact totals from the lake and overwrites them. Readers get speed now and correctness later.
The cost is two codebases computing the same thing in two engines. They drift: a bug fixed in one but not the other makes the chart jump every morning.
changes: ~ Batch job overwrites stream results nightly

steps.title: One river: kappa
body: The kappa architecture drops the batch layer. The event log keeps a long history, and everything — trending, royalty totals — is computed by stream jobs.

Need to fix a bug or add a metric? Start v2 of the job reading the log from the beginning; when it catches up, switch readers over and retire v1. One codebase, at the price of a long-retention log and replays that take hours.

callout.text: Batch is just a stream that happens to be finite. Many modern engines run the same code over both.

steps.title: Rivers and lakes: recap
body:
• Separate analytics → big scans never share a database with users
  • Batch → complete, exact and cheap, but hours behind
  • Stream → seconds fresh, with windows and checkpointed state
  • Event time + watermarks → handle late data, accept small inexactness
  • Lambda vs kappa → two pipelines for correctness, or one log you can replay
